pages.title: About
pages.content:
Frame by Frame is an independent magazine about films and television, written by critics who still get excited when the lights go down.

We review new releases every week, cover festivals from the front row, and keep watchlists for every kind of evening.

How we rate

  • ★★★★★ A film we will be talking about for years.
  • ★★★★☆ Excellent, go and see it.
  • ★★★☆☆ Good, with reservations.
  • ★★☆☆☆ For fans only.
  • ★☆☆☆☆ Stay home.

posts.title: The Salt Road
posts.excerpt: A father and daughter drive across a dried-up lake in the year's most quietly devastating road movie.
posts.content:
★★★★½ Drama · 118 min · In cinemas Friday

The Salt Road begins with a car that will not start and ends with one that will not stop, and in between it finds more feeling in silence than most films find in speeches. A retired surveyor drives his estranged daughter across a dried-up lake bed to scatter her mother's ashes, and the flat white horizon becomes the third character.

Director Ines Varo shoots almost everything from inside the car. We see the road the way they do: through a cracked windscreen, a mirror, the gap between two people who have forgotten how to talk. When the camera finally steps outside, at a petrol station at dusk, the open air feels like a held breath let go.

Two performances, one silence

The leads barely raise their voices. Their arguments happen in what they leave unsaid, in who reaches for the radio, in who pretends to sleep. By the time the daughter finally laughs at one of his terrible jokes, the cinema around me was holding its breath.

Grief, it turns out, is mostly logistics, and this film understands that better than any I can remember.

From our screening notes

Credits

Directed by Ines Varo

Written by Ines Varo & Tomas Rell

Cinematography Yuki Aram

Music Delphine Oster

The verdict

Patient, funny and wrecking. Bring someone you have been meaning to call.

comments.author: Noor Hadley
comments.content: Saw it at the festival preview. That petrol station scene.

comments.author: Felix Brandt
comments.content: The radio arguments felt so real it was uncomfortable. In a good way.

posts.title: Low Neon, season one
posts.excerpt: A rain-soaked detective series that takes its time, then takes your weekend.
posts.content:
★★★★☆ Series · 8 episodes · Streaming now

Low Neon is a detective show in the way that a jazz record is background music: technically true, and missing the point. Over eight episodes it follows a night-shift investigator through a city where it never stops raining, and the case is almost an excuse to sit in the dark with her.

The first two episodes are slow, deliberately so. Stick with them. By the third, the show's rhythm becomes hypnotic: long dialogue scenes in diners, a car parked in the same spot every night, a radio host who seems to know more than he should.

Episodes to watch twice

  • Episode 3, "Closing Time": one diner, one night, one confession.
  • Episode 5, "Static": told almost entirely over a radio call-in show.
  • Episode 8, "First Light": the rain finally stops, and everything changes.

The ending will divide people. I think it is perfect, and I have been thinking about it for a week.

comments.author: Marta Quell
comments.content: Episode 5 is the best hour of television this year.

posts.title: Dispatch from the Harbour Film Festival: day three
posts.excerpt: Outdoor screenings, a standing ovation for a documentary about bakers, and the film everyone is arguing about.
posts.content:
Day three of the Harbour Film Festival began with rain and ended with four hundred people under blankets watching a documentary about a night bakery. Nobody left early. Several people cried into their festival-issue cinnamon buns.

What we saw

  • Night Loaves: a documentary about the last 24-hour bakery in the old port. Standing ovation.
  • Tidewater: a romance told across fifty years of the same pier. Divisive, gorgeous.
  • Signal Lost: a sci-fi thriller set on a weather station. Fun, forgettable.
  • The Orchard Keepers: our favourite so far. Full review soon.

The outdoor screen on the harbour wall is the best thing about this festival. Ferries pass behind it, the wind moves the canvas, and somehow it all becomes part of the film.

Tomorrow: the shorts programme, and a midnight screening that the programmers will only describe as loud.

comments.author: Ollie Reyes
comments.content: Night Loaves needs a proper release. Please.

posts.title: The Orchard Keepers
posts.excerpt: Three generations, one failing orchard and a summer that will not end: the festival's warmest discovery.
posts.content:
★★★★☆ Drama · 104 min · Festival selection

The Orchard Keepers takes place over one hot summer, as a family decides whether to sell the orchard that has been in their name for a century. It sounds like a premise for a gentle drama, and it is, but it is also funny, sharp about money, and full of small surprises.

The grandmother refuses to discuss the sale and instead teaches everyone to graft trees. The grandson wants to film it all for his followers. The mother just wants one night of sleep. By the end, all three are right.

Why it works

The film trusts its audience. No one explains how they feel; the orchard does it for them. A dying tree in the first act gets a single line of dialogue and a payoff in the last that I will not spoil.

posts.title: Ten films for a rainy weekend
posts.excerpt: Blanket, tea, phone in another room: our critics pick the films that are better when it is pouring outside.
posts.content:
Some films are made for big screens and some are made for sofas. These are the ones we reach for when the weather has cancelled every plan, the kettle is on, and the evening is ours.

We have kept the list to films that are easy to find and impossible to regret. Start anywhere.

  1. The Long Winter: a cabin, a storm and two neighbours who hate each other. A comedy, eventually.
  2. Low Neon (the pilot): one episode, you will want more.
  3. Paper Mountains: an animated journey across a folded landscape.
  4. Night Loaves: the bakery documentary, when it arrives.
  5. The Orchard Keepers: summer, bottled.
  6. Signal Lost: a weather station, a storm, a mystery.
  7. Tidewater: for the romantics.
  8. The Salt Road: bring tissues.
  9. Velvet Hour: a musical set in one cinema over one night.
  10. Marquee: a documentary about the last single-screen cinema in town.

Disagree? Good. Tell us your rainy-day film in the comments.

comments.author: Priya Sand
comments.content: Velvet Hour forever. Watched it three times last winter.

comments.author: Noor Hadley
comments.content: Adding Paper Mountains for the kids this weekend.

posts.title: The Long Winter
posts.excerpt: Two feuding neighbours, one snowed-in cabin and the warmest comedy of the season.
posts.content:
★★★½☆ Comedy · 96 min · In cinemas

When a blizzard traps two feuding neighbours in the only cabin with a working stove, The Long Winter becomes a two-hander that is equal parts bickering and kindness. It is slight, and it knows it, but it is very good company.

The best scenes are the smallest: an argument about how to cut firewood, a shared tin of peaches, a game of cards that goes on for three days of screen time.

The film was shot in eleven days in a real cabin during a real storm, and the cold on screen is not acting. Both leads have said they have never been happier to see a wrap party.

It loses a star for an ending that ties everything up too neatly, but you will leave smiling.

posts.title: Paper Mountains
posts.excerpt: An animated journey through a folded landscape, made almost entirely from cut paper.
posts.content:
★★★★★ Animation · 88 min · Family

Every frame of Paper Mountains was cut, folded and photographed by hand, and you can feel it. The mountains have creases, the rivers ripple like tissue, and the sun is a circle of orange paper that someone clearly cut very carefully.

The story is simple: a young cartographer sets out to map a range that refolds itself every night. Children will love the creatures; adults will love the quiet way it talks about change.

For the grown-ups

Stay for the credits, which show the studio's paper workshop in time-lapse. It is the best ninety seconds of the year.

It looks like a pop-up book having a beautiful dream.

A seven-year-old at our screening

posts.title: Why we still go to the cinema
posts.excerpt: Streaming made watching easy. The cinema keeps making it matter. An essay on dark rooms and strangers.
posts.content:
There is a moment, just after the lights go down and before the first image appears, when a room full of strangers agrees to pay attention together. It lasts about two seconds. I think it is the best thing about cinema.

Streaming is wonderful. It gave us more films than we will ever watch, and it let us watch them in pyjamas. But at home a film competes with everything: the phone, the washing, the urge to check how long is left.

The shared gasp

In a cinema you hear the audience. The laugh that starts in the back row. The gasp at the twist. The silence that is not empty but full. Those reactions change the film, and you cannot get them on a sofa.

So go. Take a friend, take a stranger's recommendation, take the late show. Sit in the middle, put the phone away, and let the lights go down.

comments.author: Felix Brandt
comments.content: The two seconds before the first image. Exactly this.
